_about: AI-written (Claude) summaries built from PSI investigation metadata, PSI experiment tables and the PSI report files listed in each finding's source. Written and fact-checked against those sources on 2026-11-14 (every finding traced to a passage or computed from the table); habitat-relevance notes are interpretation. Verify against the sources before citing.

PSI-26.summary: Burned real spacecraft-type solids (cotton-fiberglass fabric, Nomex, Ultem, PMMA sheets, spheres and slabs, candles) in a small wind tunnel on the ISS, then tried to put some flames out with nitrogen.
PSI-26.engineer: First long-duration data on thick and practical solid fuels in purely forced flow. Compares directly with the 1-g NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 screening method.
PSI-26.varied: Air speed (main variable, up to 40 cm/s), flow direction (opposed vs concurrent), sample shape and size, O2 (later tests ~17% via N2)
PSI-26.fixed: ~1 atm ISS pressure, MSG duct 76 x 76 mm, hot-wire igniter
PSI-26.sensors: Video and digital still cameras (top and edge views), radiometer, flow display

findings.t: Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 did not burn at ISS 21-22% O2 and ~15 cm/s, similar to 1-g; Nomex-III did burn at 22% O2 and 14 cm/s.

In normal-gravity air this cotton-fiberglass fabric self-extinguishes when the flame must spread downward against the flow, but in microgravity it spread steadily in opposed flow, fastest at about 10-15 cm/s: enhanced flammability in space.

At 10 cm/s the flame spreading with the air flow (concurrent) moved 2.55 mm/s, twice the 1.21 mm/s of the flame spreading against it. Flames reached a steady length only below 10 cm/s, and concurrent flames went out (quenching) only when the flow dropped below about 1 cm/s.
Compared side by side, the normal-gravity concurrent flame was much longer and sootier and was still accelerating, while the microgravity flame nearly reached a steady state.

At 17% O2 and under 1 cm/s flow, a nitrogen jet failed to put out a burning 15-mm PMMA sphere; the flame went out only when the airflow was stopped. In a separate test in air, a 500 cc/min nitrogen jet weakened but did not extinguish a burning PMMA sphere.
NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 may not be conservative: materials can burn at lower O2 in microgravity, and misapplied suppressant jets can entrain air and sustain flames.

PSI-26.habitat: Directly about cabin materials and local suppression. Its tests sit at 21% or lower O2, so habitat atmospheres at 30-34% O2 are outside its envelope.
PSI-26.objective_short: Find out whether practical spacecraft solids burn in slow forced flow without buoyancy, how flames spread and go out, and whether a nitrogen jet can put them out.
PSI-26.fuel_geom: PMMA spheres 1 and 2 cm; PMMA flat samples and slabs 1-2 cm wide; cotton-fiberglass (SIBAL), Nomex and Ultem fabric strips 1-2 cm wide; candles (also lit in the wake). Mounted in the 76 x 76 mm MSG flow duct.

PSI-25.summary: Follow-on to BASS with six PI teams burning PMMA films, slabs and rods plus SIBAL fabric while lowering O2 with nitrogen to find where solids stop burning in space.
PSI-25.engineer: The best PSI dataset for microgravity flammability boundaries (O2 vs flow) of solids, with O2, CO2 and CO readings for each test.
PSI-25.varied: O2 13.6-22.2% (N2 dilution), duct air speed 0-55 cm/s, fuel thickness (100-400 µm films, slabs, 1/4-1/2 in rods), flow direction
PSI-25.sensors: Video, Nikon stills, radiometer, O2 / CO2 (CDM) / CO (CSA-CP) sensors, duct air display

findings.t: PMMA rods in concurrent stagnation flow burned down to 13.5% O2 at low stretch, well below the 15.4% upward-spread limit measured in normal gravity with an extra 4 cm/s forced flow.
Black PMMA rods spread flames in opposed flow down to 17.5% O2 in microgravity versus no spread below 19% in normal gravity.
SIBAL fabric quenching speeds were 1-5 cm/s, higher in lower O2: the first clean low-speed quenching boundary in concurrent spread.

The report calls the low-speed flow near surfaces a 'Goldilocks' zone typical of spacecraft ventilation, where materials stay flammable, and says Test 1's 25 s ignition may act as an ignition test, not a flammability test.

PSI-25.habitat: Core evidence that 1-g screening under-predicts flammability. Its boundaries are at 21% O2 or below, so extrapolating to 30-34% O2 lunar atmospheres needs modeling.
PSI-25.objective_short: Map where solids stop burning in space (limiting O2 vs air speed) and compare that boundary with NASA's 1-g screening test.
PSI-25.fuel_geom: Clear and black PMMA rods 6.3, 9.5 and 12.7 mm (1/4, 3/8, 1/2 in); PMMA films 0.1-0.4 mm thick, 1-2 cm wide; SIBAL fabric strips 1 and 2 cm wide; PMMA slabs. Same MSG flow duct.

PSI-98.summary: Burned a 94 x 40.6 cm sheet of cotton-fiberglass fabric inside an empty Cygnus cargo ship after it left the ISS: the first large-scale spacecraft fire test.
PSI-98.engineer: Answers how fast a large fire grows in low gravity and whether it reaches a steady spread rate. Few test points, very rich imagery.
PSI-98.fixed: SIBAL fabric, 20 cm/s air, ~21.5% O2, Cygnus cabin pressure
PSI-98.sensors: 2 cameras, thermocouples (flow, flame, plume), 2 radiometers, pressure / CO2 / O2 sensors, 2 anemometers

findings.t: Table: the concurrent-flow sample burned 420 s; the opposed-flow sample burned 70 s at the same 20 cm/s and ~21.5% O2.
Objective: determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and whether it reaches steady spread.

PSI-98.habitat: Only full-scale data in PSI. Its sensor suite (O2, CO2, temperatures) also gives a basis for cabin-level smoke and heat-release estimates.
PSI-98.objective_short: See how fast a large fire grows in a spacecraft-sized volume and whether it reaches a steady spread rate.
PSI-98.fuel_geom: One SIBAL cotton-fiberglass sheet, 94 x 40.6 cm, 0.37 mm thick, in a flow duct inside an uncrewed Cygnus.

PSI-99.summary: Nine 5 x 29 cm samples (SIBAL, silicone, PMMA, PMMA with Nomex) burned in the same Cygnus duct to compare low-gravity flammability with NASA's 1-g screening test.
PSI-99.engineer: Rare direct µg vs 1-g spread-rate pairs for the same materials.
PSI-99.sensors: Cameras, thermocouples, radiometers, O2/CO2 sensors, anemometers

findings.t: Table: silicone samples showed only insignificant burning in µg (some burned completely in the 1-g reference).
Table: SIBAL concurrent spread in µg was 2.1-2.6 mm/s, and the 1-g reference spread accelerated.
Table: the two PMMA-only samples burned 600 s and 900 s with flames anchored at the sample base and very slow regression (0.01-0.04 mm/s).

PSI-99.habitat: Material-by-material evidence for selection. Silicone and Nomex behavior matters for cabin seals and fabrics.
PSI-99.objective_short: Compare microgravity ignition and flame spread of nine materials with NASA's 1-g screening test.
PSI-99.fuel_geom: Nine sheets, mostly 29 x 5 cm (one 5 x 5 cm), 0.27-10 mm thick: SIBAL fabric, silicone, PMMA, PMMA with Nomex.

PSI-100.summary: A repeat of Saffire-I with the same large SIBAL sheet at a faster 30 cm/s airflow.
PSI-100.engineer: Pairs with Saffire-I to show the effect of ventilation speed on large-scale fire growth.
PSI-100.fixed: SIBAL fabric, 30 cm/s, Cygnus cabin air

findings.t: Objective (same as Saffire-I): determine large-scale fire growth rate and whether spread becomes steady, here at 30 cm/s.

PSI-100.habitat: Ventilation speed is a design variable for habitats, and this pair (20 vs 30 cm/s) brackets typical cabin flows.
PSI-100.objective_short: Repeat Saffire-I at a faster air speed to show how ventilation changes large-scale fire growth.
PSI-100.fuel_geom: SIBAL sheet 94 x 40.6 cm, 0.33 mm thick, same Cygnus flow duct.

PSI-102.summary: Heated five common spacecraft materials (Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cotton lampwick, dibutyl phthalate) to make smoke, then measured smoke particle sizes and how the ISS and Shuttle smoke detectors responded.
PSI-102.engineer: Particle size statistics (moment method) for pre-fire smoke in microgravity, plus side-by-side detector responses.
PSI-102.varied: Material, heater temperature, air flow 5 or 10 cm/s, smoke aging time (10-1800 s)
PSI-102.sensors: P-Trak particle counter, DustTrak, ionization chamber, ISS and STS smoke detectors, thermophoretic TEM samplers

findings.t: ISS (light-scattering) and Shuttle (ionization) detectors respond to different particle size ranges because both were designed from 1-g smoke data.
Teflon smoke was mostly below 1 µm: the Shuttle detector signal was strong while the ISS detector was erratic.
The report recommends detectors that measure more than one moment of the size distribution, or classify particles by size.

PSI-102.habitat: Direct input to detector requirements for Orion, Gateway and surface habitats.
PSI-102.objective_short: Measure the particle size of smoke from overheated (not burning) spacecraft materials in microgravity and how ISS and Shuttle smoke detectors respond to it.
PSI-102.fuel_geom: Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cotton lampwick and dibutyl phthalate samples on a carousel, heated by a wire to below their ignition point. No flame.

PSI-101.summary: Reflight of SAME with broader conditions (no-flow heating, higher temperatures), a new fire-retardant foam (Pyrell) and a prototype two-moment smoke detector (MPASS).
PSI-101.engineer: 66 test points. Shows how flow and heating change smoke size, and how a two-moment detector rejects dust.
PSI-101.varied: Material, heater temperature (Rt/R0), inlet velocity 0-8.1 cm/s, aging time
PSI-101.sensors: MPASS two-moment detector, DustTrak, ionization detector, P-Trak, TEM samplers

findings.t: Zero-flow heating produced smoke particles 2-3 times larger than at the nominal 8 cm/s flow.
All materials made sub-micron smoke readily seen by ionization detectors, but aged silicone smoke grew to sizes better seen by light scattering.
The prototype two-moment detector (MPASS) could tell high smoke concentration apart from a few large dust particles, cutting false alarms.

PSI-101.habitat: Lunar dust makes nuisance-alarm rejection critical, and this is the PSI dataset that addresses it.
PSI-101.objective_short: Reflight of SAME over a wider range of heating and flow, with a new foam and a prototype two-moment smoke detector.
PSI-101.fuel_geom: Kapton, silicone, lampwick, Teflon and Pyrell foam heated on a carousel to three temperature levels, with inlet flow 0-8.1 cm/s and smoke aging. No flame.

PSI-47.summary: Checked that a commercial particle counter (P-Trak), modified to recycle its alcohol by capillary action, works in microgravity, using test dust instead of smoke.
PSI-47.engineer: De-risked the SAME instruments and gives background-aerosol context for false-alarm studies.
PSI-47.fixed: Arizona Road Dust aerosol in 15 L Mylar bags

findings.t: The modified P-Trak was compared with a DustTrak using a known dust aerosol, and an impactor removed particles above the P-Trak's 2.5 µm limit.

PSI-47.habitat: Baseline for dust-vs-smoke discrimination, highly relevant for lunar regolith dust.
PSI-47.objective_short: Prove that the P-Trak particle counter, a key SAME instrument, works in long-duration microgravity; measure background particles in the ISS cabin.
PSI-47.fuel_geom: No fuel. Arizona Road Dust test aerosol in 15 L Mylar bags, plus ISS cabin air sampled at several modules. Hand-held P-Trak (with capillary alcohol wick) and DustTrak run by the crew.

PSI-69.summary: Burned single free-floating droplets of methanol and heptane in atmospheres diluted with nitrogen, CO2 or helium to measure how well inert gases suppress fires in microgravity.
PSI-69.engineer: 274 tests with measured O2, diluent, pressure, initial and extinction diameters, and burning-rate constant: a ready dataset for the limiting oxygen index vs pressure and diluent.
PSI-69.varied: O2 mole fraction, diluent (N2, CO2, He), pressure (~0.7-3 atm), droplet size 1.1-4.7 mm
PSI-69.sensors: Backlit droplet camera, OH* UV camera, color video, radiometers

findings.t: Lowest oxygen that keeps a droplet burning (limiting oxygen index) at 1 atm: 12% for methanol and 15% for heptane in O2/N2. With CO2 added to air to simulate a suppressant it rose to about 14% and 17%; with helium added, about 14% and 15%.

Methanol droplets still ignited and burned briefly at 13% O2 (rest N2) at 1 atm. At 18% O2 or more, flames went out by diffusive extinction at small droplet sizes; at 14% or less, by radiative extinction close to the starting size. More CO2 favoured radiative extinction, as expected from its strong infrared emission.

n-heptane, n-octane and n-decane droplets (14-25% O2, 0.5-1 atm, CO2- or helium-diluted) all kept burning with an invisible 'cool flame' after the visible flame went out radiatively; cool-flame burning rates were slightly lower than hot-flame rates.
FLEX was the first experiment run in the Combustion Integrated Rack. NASA's 2009-2011 data report says the measured limiting oxygen values came out slightly lower than initially expected.
The flammability limit is lower in reduced gravity, so inert-suppressant standards set on Earth may not give the same safety margin in space.
Heptane droplets kept vaporizing after visible flame extinction, sustained by a 'cool flame'. The Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) later followed this up.
Table: 186 tests ended in extinction, 61 in disruption and 27 burned to completion.

Table: 17 FLEX tests (heptane and methanol) ran at 30-34% O2 and 10.3-10.5 psi, close to the planned lunar-habitat atmosphere (30% O2, 10.2 psi); 15 ended in droplet disruption and 2 burned to completion. All 17 ran in 2009-2010 with coated fuel needles; NASA's data report says methanol disruptions in that period were probably caused by the needle coating.

PSI-69.habitat: Supports choosing CO2 vs N2 vs He suppressants for pressure-reduced habitats, and it is the only PSI flight dataset with tests run at the planned lunar-habitat atmosphere (30-34% O2 near 10.3 psi), although with liquid droplets, not solids.
PSI-69.objective_short: Measure how pressure and inert diluents (N2, CO2, He) change droplet burning and the oxygen limit, to rank suppressants for spacecraft.
PSI-69.fuel_geom: Free-floating methanol and heptane droplets, 1.1-4.7 mm initial diameter, deployed and ignited in the MDCA inside the CIR.

PSI-68.summary: Extended FLEX to real fuels and mixtures (octanes, decane, ethanol, propanol-glycerol), slow flows and fiber-supported droplets.
PSI-68.engineer: Wide atmosphere range: O2 17-30%, 0.5-3 atm. The PSI table is only a test-matrix summary, so per-test data sit in publications.
PSI-68.varied: Fuel and mixtures, O2 17-30%, pressure 0.5-3 atm, flow 0.1-5 cm/s, N2 or He diluent

findings.t: In 1 atm air on the ISS, n-heptane, n-octane and n-decane droplets larger than about 2 mm often lost their visible flame through radiative heat loss, and burning slowed toward plain evaporation. Estimated flame temperature fell from above 1200 K to under about 800 K and then held steady, which the authors linked to a low-temperature (cool-flame) burning regime.

iso-Octane droplets smaller than 2.7 mm burned to completion; larger ones went out radiatively, with flame radiation dropping about a hundredfold and the flame flickering. Estimated flame temperature fell from about 1600 K to about 700 K after the flame went out. Unlike n-heptane, it is unclear whether iso-octane enters a cool-flame regime: its burning rate simply decayed toward evaporation.

A 50/50 n-heptane/iso-octane mix (a gasoline reference fuel) kept a normal hot flame below 3 mm. Larger droplets went out radiatively and switched to cool-flame burning, with an abrupt drop in burning rate. Neither component evaporated preferentially, and a detailed model with low-temperature chemistry matched the ISS measurements.

FLEX-2's 'surrogate fuel' tests burned free n-heptane, n-octane and n-decane droplets in 1 atm air. A 2026 study used 19,537 of these flame images to automate flame-diameter measurement with an AI segmentation model (3.1% mean error against manual measurement, about 229 times faster).
Table: the PSI table lists the planned test matrix (17-30% O2, 0.5-3 atm, flow 0.1-5 cm/s), not per-test results; those are in the 48 listed publications.

PSI-68.habitat: Its high-O2, low-pressure corner overlaps the planned lunar habitat atmosphere.
PSI-68.objective_short: Extend FLEX to practical and multicomponent liquid fuels, fiber-supported droplets and slow forced flows.
PSI-68.fuel_geom: Droplets 1.5-5 mm, free or on a fiber: heptane, n-octane, iso-octane, decane, ethanol, propanol-glycerol and heptane/iso-octane blends.

PSI-39.summary: Studied the 'cool flames' found in FLEX using dodecane and dodecane / iso-dodecane droplets across a wide pressure range, with and without helium.
PSI-39.engineer: Low-temperature chemistry data. Cool flames are nearly invisible and can re-ignite, a hidden hazard.
PSI-39.varied: Pressure 0.5-5 atm, O2 17-21%, helium, fuel blend, free vs fiber droplet
PSI-39.sensors: B/W droplet camera, UV OH* camera, color camera

findings.t: Cool flames need long residence times and cannot be observed with droplet flames in normal gravity.
Cool-flame extinction occurs when static stability is lost near the lower turnover point of the negative-temperature-coefficient region.

PSI-39.habitat: Flags a detection gap: cool flames emit little light or heat.
PSI-39.objective_short: Study 'cool flames' (low-temperature burning) of large-alkane droplets and when they start and go out, across pressure.
PSI-39.fuel_geom: n-dodecane and dodecane/iso-dodecane droplets, free-floating or fiber-supported, in the MDCA.

PSI-20.summary: A porous gas burner whose fuel flow is set to mimic how paper, plastic or alcohol would burn, tested in still air at O2 up to 40%.
PSI-20.engineer: Emulates solid-fuel flammability in quiescent environments as a function of material properties, the configuration most like a sealed habitat with fans off.
PSI-20.varied: O2 21-40%, burner 25 or 50 mm, fuel (C2H4, 50% C2H4, CH4), pressure 0.56-1 bar (not tabulated in PSI; from Dehghani & Quintiere 2023)
PSI-20.sensors: Heat-flux gauge, surface thermocouples, cameras, radiometers

findings.t: 49 ethylene flames on the 25 mm burner burned steadily on the ISS at 26.5-40% O2 and 0.56-1 bar, the range considered for spacecraft atmospheres. Oxygen fraction dominated whether a flame kept burning; pressure over 0.56-1 atm had a relatively negligible effect.

For each O2 level, steady burning sits inside a window of heat of combustion versus heat of gasification: above it flames go out by radiation loss (radiant fraction above about 0.65, large flames), below it by a 'small flame' limit like Earth's fire point (about 40 kW/m2 critical heat release). Steady flames needed about 1100-1200 K; real solid and liquid fuels fall inside these limits, so they could also burn steadily in microgravity.
Theory for PMMA shows that external radiant heating (for example from a nearby fire or hot surface) can allow steady burning where it was otherwise impossible, including at 21% O2.

On the ISS, low-momentum emulator flames burned for minutes with no air flow and no flame spread, but self-extinguished at O2 below about 25%. Larger flames generally went out within 1.5 minutes, and methane flames within a minute.

The ISS tests mimicked plastics by matching heats of combustion and gasification, surface temperature and smoke point, and included the elevated-O2, reduced-pressure atmospheres considered for future crew vehicles.

Before flight, 5-second drop-tower tests with 25 and 50 mm burners gave a roughly hemispherical flame with near-steady heat flux after about 5 s; the larger burner burned faster than pure-diffusion theory predicts, showing gas radiation matters.
Designed to assess whether existing flammability tests apply in low- and partial-gravity environments.
Table: tests reached 34% and 40% O2, the range of planned exploration atmospheres.

PSI-20.habitat: The strongest PSI match for 30-40% O2 habitats and for zero-ventilation scenarios.
PSI-20.objective_short: Emulate how solid materials burn in still air, and where they stop burning, as a function of material properties, using a controllable gas burner.
PSI-20.fuel_geom: Flat porous burners 25 or 50 mm diameter fed ethylene, 50% ethylene or methane; fuel flow set to mimic the heat of gasification of a chosen solid.

PSI-159.summary: Spherical 'cool diffusion flames' of ethane, propane and butane, including inverse flames with an oxidizer of up to 85% O2 blown into a fuel-filled chamber.
PSI-159.engineer: Holds the highest O2 concentrations in PSI, along with ignition, self-extinction and hot-ignition outcomes for each test.
PSI-159.varied: Fuel, normal vs inverse flame, O2 (ambient 18-40%, burner stream to 85%), pressure ~0.5-3.3 atm, flow rate
PSI-159.sensors: ACME DataCam, CFI intensified camera with formaldehyde filter, HiBMs camera, radiometers, PMTs, thermocouples

findings.t: Spherical cool diffusion flames burning gases were observed for the first time, but only for normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with 39% ambient O2; they were not readily produced.
In related normal-gravity ground tests, cool diffusion flames burning near the surface of fuel pools were observed for the first time.

PSI-159.habitat: Data at oxygen-rich conditions comparable to suit and O2-line leak scenarios.
PSI-159.objective_short: Create and study cool diffusion flames of gaseous fuels, including inverse flames, and measure their ignition and extinction.
PSI-159.fuel_geom: 6.35 mm porous spherical burner. Normal flames: ethane, propane or butane (pure or N2-diluted) flow out into O2/N2. Inverse flames: O2/N2 with up to 85% O2 flows out into a fuel-filled chamber.

PSI-10.summary: Spherical ethylene and propane flames in O2-enriched air, normal and inverse, to learn how to 'design' flames that are robust and soot-free.
PSI-10.engineer: Extinction and soot limits as a function of stoichiometric mixture fraction (Zst) at O2 20-40%: useful for fire models at high O2.
PSI-10.varied: O2 20-40% (inverse burner stream to 85%), pressure ~0.4-3 atm, fuel dilution, Zst, flow

findings.t: By varying Zst at constant flame temperature, flames were made that stay soot-free at any strain rate ('permanently blue'), with extinction scalar dissipation rates up to 40 times those of fuel-air flames.

PSI-10.habitat: Shows how O2 enrichment changes soot and extinction, which matter for smoke detection at 30-34% O2.
PSI-10.objective_short: Learn which flame structure (stoichiometric mixture fraction, O2) gives robust, soot-free flames; measure extinction and soot limits.
PSI-10.fuel_geom: 6.35 mm porous spherical burner, normal and inverse; ethylene and propane diluted with N2.

PSI-23.summary: Spherical hydrogen, methane and ethylene flames from a porous sphere, run until radiative extinction, in N2- or He-diluted air at ~21% and ~30% O2.
PSI-23.engineer: Clean 1-D extinction data for validating detailed chemistry and radiation models.
PSI-23.varied: Fuel blend, O2 ~21 or ~30%, diluent N2 vs He, flow rate

findings.t: Radiative extinction could not be reached in 2.2-s or 5-s drop towers or parabolic flights; on the ISS, 20% C2H4 / 80% N2 burned quasi-steadily at 3 cc/s, while 5-10 cc/s led to radiative extinction.

PSI-23.habitat: Model-validation data for fire simulation codes at 21-30% O2.
PSI-23.objective_short: Measure radiative extinction of spherical diffusion flames to test chemistry and radiation models.
PSI-23.fuel_geom: 6.35 mm porous spherical burner; hydrogen, methane, ethylene and blends, diluted with N2 or He.

PSI-21.summary: Coflow laminar methane and ethylene flames, from dilute near-extinction to heavily sooting, to improve soot models.
PSI-21.varied: Fuel and N2 dilution, fuel and coflow rates
PSI-21.sensors: OH*/CH* chemiluminescence, soot luminosity, laser extinction, thin-filament pyrometry

findings.t: Preliminary ISS results: soot volume fraction can be several times higher in microgravity than in comparable 1-g flames, and the flames are taller and wider.
Dilution limits for methane and ethylene flames were extended in microgravity: flames were more stable, so lifted flames held at lower fuel concentrations.
Table: per-test-day log only (no per-test results); results above come from the papers.

PSI-21.habitat: Indirect: soot models feed smoke-detection and radiation predictions.
PSI-21.objective_short: Measure coflow laminar flames from near-extinction to heavily sooting to improve soot models.
PSI-21.fuel_geom: Coflow burner (fuel tube inside a concentric air tube); methane and ethylene, N2-diluted.

PSI-22.summary: Applied up to 10 kV between burner and a mesh to see how electric fields push the ions in flames. The field acts like an artificial buoyancy.
PSI-22.engineer: The only PSI investigation that mimics partial gravity, using ion-driven flow in place of buoyancy.
PSI-22.varied: Field polarity and strength, fuel (CH4, C2H4) and dilution, coflow vs jet burner
PSI-22.sensors: Ion current, cameras, flame response time

findings.t: Unlike in 1 g, microgravity flames showed a distinct peak in ion current matching the most compact flame. Soot generation could be suppressed, and flame luminosity, combustion intensity and ion current were clearly correlated.
Highly diluted flames could be stabilized with very weak electric fields, but strong fields caused corona and arc discharges.
Table: per-test-day log only (no per-test results); results above come from the papers.

PSI-22.habitat: A proxy for lunar and Martian gravity until LUCI and FM2 data enter PSI.
PSI-22.objective_short: Use an electric field acting on flame ions to steer flames, as a stand-in for buoyancy.
PSI-22.fuel_geom: Coflow and gas-jet burners facing a high-voltage mesh (up to 10 kV); methane and ethylene, N2-diluted.

PSI-107.summary: Small gas-jet flames in co-flowing air, with fuel flow increased until the flame started to emit soot (the 'smoke point').
PSI-107.engineer: 52 smoke points for ethylene, propane, propylene and mixtures: a sooting-propensity scale for microgravity fires.
PSI-107.varied: Fuel, nozzle 0.41/0.76/1.6 mm, coflow 5.4-65 cm/s, fuel flow
PSI-107.sensors: Still and video cameras, radiometer, flow sensors

findings.t: Higher coflow shortens luminous flames but moves smoke points to higher fuel flows and longer flames.
Smoke-point length scaled with burner diameter to the -0.91 power times coflow velocity to the 0.41 power.
Propane showed an unusually high sooting propensity in microgravity.

PSI-107.habitat: Smoke yield of fires depends on ventilation, which matters for detection timing.
PSI-107.objective_short: Measure smoke points of gas-jet flames in coflowing air to rank how readily fuels soot in microgravity.
PSI-107.fuel_geom: Round nozzles 0.41, 0.76 and 1.60 mm inner diameter in the SPICE coflow duct; ethylene, propane, propylene, methane and N2-diluted propylene.

PSI-106.summary: Studied when and how microgravity jet flames lift off the burner and blow out, using the SPICE duct.
PSI-106.engineer: Liftoff and blowout limits vs fuel, burner and coflow.
PSI-106.varied: Fuel and N2 dilution, burner tube, coflow
PSI-106.sensors: High-resolution stills with overlaid sensor data (4,000+ images)

findings.t: Microgravity methane coflow flames were about 4 to 8 times sootier (peak soot volume fraction) than the same flames at 1 g. Peak soot moved from the centerline (1 g) to the flame wings (microgravity), and flame temperature was lower in microgravity because of soot radiation.

Flame size is set mainly by the fuel mass flow rate; nonbuoyant flames are noticeably longer than at 1 g, while fuel dilution and inlet velocity matter less. Models still underestimate soot volume fraction, most of all in microgravity.
Table: per-test-day log only (no per-test results); results above come from the papers.

PSI-106.objective_short: Measure when jet flames lift off the nozzle and blow out in coflowing air.
PSI-106.fuel_geom: Coflow jet burner in the SPICE duct; methane, ethane and ethylene, pure or N2-diluted.

PSI-62.summary: Ground study: new flamelet (FGM) models of concurrent flame spread checked against 3-D soot and temperature reconstructed from BASS and BASS-II images.
PSI-62.engineer: A validated modeling route for the BASS data.
PSI-62.sensors: Two-color tomography of PSI DSLR images

findings.t: Uses PSI imagery from BASS and BASS-II to reconstruct soot and temperature fields for model comparison.

PSI-62.objective_short: Model concurrent flame spread over solids with flamelet chemistry and check it against BASS and BASS-II images.
PSI-62.fuel_geom: No new samples: BASS and BASS-II sample geometries, simulated.

PSI-115.summary: Ground study: simulated how smoke particles form and grow in microgravity vs Earth, in a SAME-like geometry.
PSI-115.engineer: Explains why microgravity smoke differs: no settling and no buoyant asymmetry.

findings.t: Without buoyancy or settling, microgravity smoke contained very large particles (> 40 µm), while on Earth settling capped the maximum near 40 µm and the mode near 5 µm.

PSI-115.habitat: Supports larger-particle detection channels for space detectors.
PSI-115.objective_short: Simulate how smoke particles form and grow in microgravity compared with Earth.
PSI-115.fuel_geom: Simulated dibutyl phthalate smoke in a SAME-like heater geometry.

PSI-60.summary: Ground study: soot temperature and volume fraction extracted from 1,600+ SPICE images and compared with soot models.
PSI-60.engineer: Quantitative soot fields from SPICE flights.

findings.t: Turns SPICE raw images into soot temperature and volume-fraction fields.

PSI-60.objective_short: Extract soot temperature and soot volume fraction from SPICE flight images and compare with soot models.

PSI-142.summary: Ground study using FLEX conditions to map cool-flame flammability limits with ozone-assisted counterflow flames and models.
PSI-142.engineer: Cool-flame limit diagrams that include radiation, diffusion and convection.

findings.t: Lists 8 derived datasets with the paper and figure they reproduce.

PSI-142.objective_short: Map cool-flame flammability limits at FLEX-like conditions with ground experiments and models.
PSI-142.fuel_geom: Ozone-assisted counterflow flames in a ground laboratory.

PSI-117.summary: Ground study: 3-D CFD of droplet cool flames validated on FLEX data, including how drift and heating perturb them.
PSI-117.engineer: Stability maps for cool-flame onset, persistence and quenching.

findings.t: Built stability maps for cool-flame ignition, oscillation, hot ignition and extinction, reconciled with FLEX.

PSI-117.objective_short: Simulate droplet cool flames in 3-D and check against FLEX.

PSI-98: Investigation dates on PSI (2001-2008) match SAME's exactly. Saffire-I actually flew on Cygnus OA-6 in June 2016 (NASA NTRS 20170002628), so the PSI dates look copied.
Two key documents (Objectives/Status PDF) fail to download from PSI (storage error).
PSI-100: The 47th ICES presentation link on PSI returns 'not found'.
PSI-26: BASS Final Report link on PSI returns 'not found'.
PSI-39: PSI description says 0.25-0.5 atm, while the experiment table lists 0.5-5 atm.
PSI-107: Description says 526 flames and coflow 5.4-65 cm/s; the table has 435 unique rows (after removing 34 duplicates) with coflow from -5.9 to 85 cm/s.
No start or end dates on the PSI page.
PSI-25: Per the BASS-II ReadMe, the video date display is one day later than the actual date (leap-year bug).
PSI-69: Burning-rate column header says 'mm', but values fit a burning-rate constant in mm²/s.

NASA's FLEX data report (2009-2011, the period in this PSI table) says a conformal coating on the fuel needles contaminated some droplets: methanol 'disruption' outcomes were probably caused by it and heptane disruptions may have been; burning rates and radiative-extinction sizes were not affected. The UV flame camera window was also smudged early on, adding uncertainty to flame sizes.

incidents.name: Apollo 1
incidents.what: Flash fire in the Command Module during a launch-pad test in a 100% O2 cabin. The crew died of carbon monoxide and toxic gases, and their burns were likely survivable.
incidents.lessons: Restrict combustibles, single quick-opening hatch, fire-resistant suits.

incidents.name: Apollo 13
incidents.what: An O2 tank exploded after pre-launch overheating (~1,000 °F) damaged the Teflon wire insulation inside it.
incidents.lessons: Recertify O2 systems, sheath wiring in stainless steel, upgrade thermostats.

incidents.name: Mir
incidents.what: A solid-fuel O2 generator burned for minutes and sent out dense smoke, blocking access to one Soyuz. Latex glove material was the likely culprit.
incidents.lessons: Ground preparation of O2 canisters, crew training, redundant O2 generation on the ISS.

incidents.name: Artemis II
incidents.what: A smoke detector tripped on Orion on the second-to-last day of the lunar flyby mission, with the crew still about 80,000 miles from home.
incidents.lessons: Detection reliability and false-alarm handling matter in deep space.

spinoffs.name: Firefighter air tanks
spinoffs.what: About 20 lb backpack, 30 min of air, about 13 lb lighter, with 4,500 psi composite-wrapped tanks from spacesuit work.

spinoffs.name: Incipient fire detector
spinoffs.what: Shuttle-derived sensor that detects combustion particles before flame or smoke and ignores dust. Used in mines.

spinoffs.name: Project FIRES
spinoffs.what: Spacesuit-derived fire-resistant, heat-protective materials for firefighter gear.

spinoffs.name: Water-mist extinguisher
spinoffs.what: From the Mist experiment (STS-107). Non-toxic water-mist units began replacing CO2 extinguishers on the ISS.

gaps_external.name: LUCI (2025)
gaps_external.what: First >25 s simulated lunar-gravity burns (spinning New Shepard). SIBAL and PMMA rod spread rates.

gaps_external.name: FM2 (planned late 2026)
gaps_external.what: First combustion experiment on the Moon: 4 solid samples in quiescent habitable atmosphere. Will look for the flammability limit at 8.2 psia.

gaps_external.name: SoFIE (GEL, MIST)
gaps_external.what: CIR insert for solid fuels at 10-40% O2, 0.2-1.5 atm, 0-30 cm/s. Results not yet in PSI.

families.CIR + ACME: The six ACME experiments (BRE, CFI-G, Flame Design, s-Flame, CLD Flame, E-FIELD Flames). All burned gaseous fuels with the same modular ACME hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), so burners, cameras and chamber are shared.
families.CIR + MDCA (droplets): FLEX, FLEX-2 and CFI burned droplets of liquid fuel in the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) inside the CIR: same chamber, droplet deployment and cameras.
families.MSG flow duct (SPICE hardware): BASS, BASS-II, SPICE and SLICE used the modular fan-driven flow duct built for SPICE, inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG). Together they cover solid and gaseous fuels in the same flow channel.
families.Saffire (Cygnus): Large samples burned in a flow duct inside uncrewed Cygnus cargo ships after they left the ISS.
families.SAME smoke hardware (MSG): SAME and SAME-R heated materials in the MSG to make smoke, then measured particle size and detector response.
families.Hand-held aerosol counters (ISS cabin): DAFT and DAFT-2 were crew-run checks of hand-held particle counters in the ISS cabin, using dust instead of smoke.
families.Ground analysis: Ground studies that model or re-analyse the flight data.

shared_links.note: The same type of instrument detected dust in DAFT/DAFT-2 and smoke in SAME and SAME-R. DAFT was flown first to show it works in microgravity.

shared_links.what: SPICE flow duct in the MSG
shared_links.note: Same fan-driven duct for solid fuels (BASS, BASS-II) and gas-jet flames (SPICE, SLICE).

shared_links.what: ACME modular hardware in the CIR
shared_links.note: Six gaseous-flame experiments, one set of hardware. BRE used it to emulate solids.

shared_links.what: MDCA droplet apparatus in the CIR
shared_links.note: Three droplet investigations with the same apparatus; CFI followed up the cool flames FLEX discovered.
